newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Ocampo sees second-half growth spurt.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Ocampo sees second-half growth spurt.

text.p: Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo said Colombia's economy should start picking up steam again in the second half of 1997, with a boost in demand fueled by lower interest rates.

"There will be a firm recovery in the second half of the year, and it wouldn't be bad to help this along with an additional cut in interest rates," Ocampo told a seminar on the country's financial and economic outlook.
Colombia's economy grew by just 2.08 percent in 1996, its lowest expansion since 1991.

Tight monetary policy, and political uncertainty stemminng from the drug corruption scandal involving President Ernesto Samper, are among factors that slowed the economy last year and drove urban unemployment to a nine-year high of 12.7 percent in the first quarter of 1997, economic analysts say.

Interest rates have dropped nine percentage points over the last year, but they are still hovering well above the levels seen in 1995 and 1994, when Colombia's economic growth rate totaled 5.36 percent and 5.8 percent, respectively. Ocampo, who sits on the central bank's board of directors, said rates would ease further in the near future, however.

His comments were supported by Leonardo Villar, another member of the bank's board, who told the seminar that lower inflationary pressures on the economy "lead us to be optimistic about the possibility of lowering interest rates."
The central bank's key overnight lending rate is currently set at 21.5 percent. Ocampo has proposed that it be trimmed to 19.5 percent.

Ocampo gave no first-quarter growth figures, but he said "the economic situation right now is one of stability." He added that the economy showed "mixed tendencies" in January-March but did not elaborate. ((-- Tom Brown, Bogota newsroom, 571 610 7944))
